
=================================================================
#56 Exile  (655)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: mugun · tone: exile drama — into island folklore
Logline: Three years of mourning, by the rite. Everyone in Sabi knows exactly what can be done inside them.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ **Queen Satek** dies, and the king, her son, loses the right to say no.
[1] [MAP 655: ]
[2] ¶ Three years of mourning, by the rite. The king may not judge, may not sign, may not overturn. Everyone in Sabi knows exactly how long three years is, and exactly what can be done inside them.
[3] ❝QUOTE (Stele of Satek Jijeok (砂宅智積碑), Buyeo, 654 — Buyeo National Museum) [Minister Satek]: Ninth day of the first month, year of the Wood Tiger. Satek Jijuk of Naji Fortress, grieving that the body’s days go so easily and its months come back so hard, cut gold to build a precious hall and carved jade to raise a treasure pagoda.❞
[4] ¶ Minister Satek carved that last year, grieving his own short days. He knows what mourning is good for.
[5] ¶ The Queen was Satek. Her death removes the clan’s hand from the king’s sleeve, and the clan understands, before the funeral rites are finished, that the sleeve is now free.
[6] ¶ With her gone, the clan has one worry left. The king owns a man who cannot be bought: Hundred-Victories **Gyebek**. And Gyebek owns a horse.
[7] ¶ They have watched him work. On the border, Gyebek earned his nickname mostly one way. He leaves the line to other men and goes looking for the general. His black horse, Gomanari, is the fastest thing on four legs in Samhan. Gyebek rides him flat along the neck like a thrown knife, the blade reversed along his forearm. The general sees a black shape where the field was empty. He starts to turn his horse, and does not finish turning. One cut on the pass. By the time the escort draws, the black horse is a speck on the far ridge. An army stands in a field with nobody left to tell it what to do.
[8] Elder Satek: He doesn’t ride at armies. / He rides at one man. / When the mourning’s over, whose house do you suppose that horse turns toward.
[9] ¶ Gyebek has no clan. That is the whole problem. He has a wife the king found for him, and a boy and a girl who carry the name the king made up. He took the wife and the name the way he takes orders, and has kept both. A man with a clan can be bargained with: you find out what his family wants and give them some of it. A man with no clan wants only what the king wants, and there is nothing to buy.
[10] ── SCENE: The Monastery ──
[11] ¶ So the two largest houses in Baekje meet, which has not happened in living memory except across a body.
[12] ¶ They meet at night, at a monastery that belongs to neither of them, and each brings the same number of men, counted twice at the gate by both sides.
[13] Elder Satek: Lord Yunbi. How many generations have we been at this?
[14] Elder Yunbi: Four. / Two of the three who died at the lantern festival last year were my nephews.
[15] Elder Satek: One of them was my grandson.
[16] ¶ Neither of them apologises. Nobody expected it and it would have ended the meeting.
[17] ¶ Halfway through the wine, a servant finds a second set of footprints behind the monastery screen — too small for the counted guards, too careful for a pilgrim. Yunbi’s man and Satek’s man look at each other and, for once, do not accuse. Someone is listening for a third house. Or for the king.
[18] Elder Satek: Spill the cups. / Tonight the doors matter more than the words.
[19] Elder Yunbi: So why did you send for me tonight.
[20] Elder Satek: His Majesty has more than forty sons. / Where do you imagine he means to seat them.
[21] Elder Yunbi: …In our chairs.
[22] Elder Satek: In the chairs of all eight houses.
[23] ¶ It goes quiet. Outside, the two sets of men are standing apart in the courtyard, arranged by habit into the shape of a fight.
[24] Elder Yunbi: We will destroy each other and lose everything. / …For how long.
[25] Elder Satek: As long as it takes. / After that we go back to the way we were.
[26] Elder Yunbi: Agreed. / What gets removed first.
[27] Elder Satek: The one with no house.
[28] ¶ They do not say his name at the table. Two houses that have not agreed on anything since before the capital moved agree, in under an hour, on one soldier with no family — and the agreement is written down nowhere, because agreements like that never are.
[29] Elder Satek: There is no price on that man.
[30] Elder Satek: Things without a price get removed.
[31] ── SCENE: The Offer ──
[32] ¶ They try the ordinary way first: they offer him a name. A real one, an old one, the eighth branch of a minor house, papers and a grave-line and ancestors, and a clan chair at the end of it for his son. It is a serious offer, and it is the only thing he has ever wanted.
[33] Elder Satek: Think of the boy. / He grows up with a name the king invented. Every door in Sabi will know it.
[34] Gyebek: I have thought of him. / …I already have one.
[35] Elder Satek: The king made that one up.
[36] Gyebek: Yes. Which is why it is owed to someone.
[37] ── SCENE: The Drill Ground ──
[38] ¶ The arrow comes through a tent wall at the Ungjin drill ground and takes the man standing next to him, who was taller. Nobody is ever charged. The fletching is Baekje army issue, which narrows it to about nine thousand people, which is the point of using it.
[39] ¶ He stops eating food he has not watched being cooked. He sleeps in a different room each night, which the ministers immediately report to the regency as the behaviour of a man planning something.
[40] ¶ One minister comes to see him: Sungchung, the man at court who asks the questions nobody else will.
[41] Sungchung: General. You should be away from here. / Half a year. Until His Majesty is out of mourning.
[42] Gyebek: …I don’t run.
[43] Sungchung: Which is exactly how they win.
[44] ¶ The truce holds exactly as long as it needs to. Four generations of blood, suspended for the length of one signature, and both houses will go back to burning each other’s carts before the year is out.
[45] ── SCENE: The Sealed Order ──
[46] ¶ Gyebek is summoned to the hall and told to kneel, and the order is read out over his head.
[47] ¶ The order is genuine. That is the craftsmanship of it. It bears the royal seal, because a king in mourning leaves his seal with the Assembly so that the country does not stop, and the Assembly has had it for four months.
[48] ¶ It is read with the king’s formula and the king’s seal, but not in the king’s voice. **Minister Satek** holds the Assembly’s borrowed stamp.
[49] Minister Satek: The seal is set. / I read this in the Assembly’s name. / Gyebek is hereby sent into exile!
[50] Satek Chunbok: …It is His Majesty’s will.
[51] ¶ Remember the young Satek who just called it His Majesty’s will. He has small feet, and he walks very carefully. He will say worse things in His Majesty’s name, later, to a much bigger king.
[52] Gyebek: His Majesty is in mourning. / He cannot will anything.
[53] ¶ Nobody answers him. He is correct, and it is not the kind of correct that helps.
[54] ¶ He is put on the boat the same afternoon. Satek water at the berth; a Yunbi winter contract in the captain’s sleeve. Even exile borrows a clan harbour.
[55] ¶ His wife is at the berth with a bundle and both children. Nobody sent for her. In Sabi, news of a sealed order travels faster than the order.
[56] Gyebek’s Wife: How long.
[57] Gyebek: I do not know.
[58] Gyebek’s Wife: Guess. For the children. / Say any number.
[59] Gyebek: I do not know the number. / I will not give them a wrong one.
[60] Gyebek’s Wife: …No. You wouldn’t.
[61] ¶ The boy asks if Father is going to war. Gyebek says no, because it is not a war. It is the only question all day he can answer exactly.
[62] ── SCENE: Sabi ──
[63] ¶ In Sabi, the order comes back to the king that evening, to be filed. That is the insult. His own seal sits at the bottom, a little crooked.
[64] King Euija: Who. / Who used my seal — / Who took my man —
[65] Minister Satek: Your Majesty… the Assembly— / In mourning the council—
[66] King Euija: Minister Satek! / I swear I’ll just— overturn the whole lot of them like Gesomun did!! / You put my man on a boat? You used my mourning as a gap?
[67] King Euija: Minister. How many days are left of my rite?
[68] Minister Satek: …Nine hundred and seventy-two, Majesty.
[69] King Euija: Good. Count them. Out loud, at my door, every morning, so I never lose one. / The morning it reaches nothing, I call the Assembly. All eight houses. Every chair. / Then I send a boat. Well? Start.
[70] Minister Satek: …Nine hundred and seventy-two.
[71] ¶ Euija laughs first, the way he always does. Then he makes the minister say it again.
[72] ── SCENE: Tamla ──
[73] ¶ He wakes on a beach with sand in his teeth and no idea how many days it has been. The not-knowing is worse than the beach.
[74] [PLACE mugun: The island where Baekje sends men it can’t afford to kill.]
[75] [CARD Yuri Dora: Yuri Dora, king of Tamla. He tells stories to men nobody else will talk to.]
[76] Gyebek: How many days.
[77] Yuri Dora: Ah. Not one for greetings, then.
[78] Gyebek: …How many days.
[79] Yuri Dora: Eleven. Better?
[80] ¶ It is better. Visibly. The islanders will spend five years noticing that this man is calmed by numbers and unsettled by almost everything else.
[81] ¶ He takes eleven from a number he has carried since the hall.
[82] Gyebek: Nine hundred and sixty-one.
[83] Yuri Dora: Until what?
[84] Gyebek: Until His Majesty can sign again. / Then he sends for me.
[85] Yuri Dora: Ha. A man who carries his own calendar. / Your name?
[86] Gyebek: I am called Gyebek.
[87] Yuri Dora: Gyebek? Like geobuk? A man named Turtle?
[88] Gyebek: No. _Gye_ is the stone step, and _baek_ is the eldest.
[89] Yuri Dora: …It was a joke.
[90] Gyebek: …Ah.
[91] ¶ He says _ah_ the way another man would say _I will write that down_. It would be a mistake to read the pause as slowness; somewhere behind those eyes, a ledger has just gained a line.
[92] ¶ **First night on the island. A fire, two cups, and a storyteller who never asks permission. “Sit or don’t. Once there were two suns…”**

=================================================================
#57 Heaven–Earth King  (태초)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · tone: island folklore
Logline: In the beginning there were two suns, two moons, and nobody ever got a decent night’s sleep.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The first night, the king of Tamla pours two cups. His guest stays by the door, busy being wronged.
[1] ¶ Yuri Dora has a fire going and no plan to ask permission.
[2] Gyebek: The order was not his. / It had his seal. It was not his.
[3] Yuri Dora: That’s the third time tonight.
[4] Gyebek: The fourth.
[5] Yuri Dora: Ha. Then you want the one about a world stolen fair and square. / I’ll start at the beginning. / Sit or don’t.
[6] ¶ **Gyebek** stays standing by the door. Yuri Dora starts anyway.
[7] ── SCENE: Two Suns ──
[8] ¶ In the beginning there were two suns and two moons. By day people dropped in the fields with their hoes still in their hands; by night they froze in their own doorways. Nobody ever had a decent night’s sleep or a decent harvest, and the old died faster than anyone could bury them.
[9] ¶ Above all of it sat **Heaven–Earth King**, who ran the living and the dead out of one office and therefore never went home. One night he fell asleep at the desk anyway, and dreamed he was eating: one sun, one moon, swallowed whole, one of each.
[10] [CARD Heaven–Earth King: The god with two jobs and one desk. He dreams about breakfast.]
[11] Heaven–Earth King: ……Huh. / One each. / I ate one of each. / Ha— that’s a son. Someone’s going to shoot those down.
[12] ¶ He comes down to the world to find the mother of that dream, and finds her in the poorest house on the road: a girl the village calls **the Lady of Wisdom**, a hearth with no fire in it, and a rice jar she does not open in front of guests.
[13] Lady of Wisdom: Who are you.
[14] Heaven–Earth King: Someone passing. / A hungry one.
[15] Lady of Wisdom: ……Sit, then.
[16] ¶ She goes round the back and lifts the lid of the jar. The bottom of it looks up at her. She puts the lid back as if that might help, ties up her hair, and walks across the road.
[17] ¶ Across the road lives **Sumyung Jangja**, who is rich the way a flood is wet. He has nine storehouses, a horse that kicks beggars, a dog that bites whatever the horse misses, and a rice measure that comes out a little smaller when he lends and a little larger when he collects.
[18] Lady of Wisdom: Lend me one measure of rice. / I have a guest.
[19] [CARD Sumyung Jangja: The richest man under two suns. He lends one measure and collects two.]
[20] Sumyung Jangja: One measure. / Two when you pay it back. / A guest? Anyone who’d come to your house, I can guess.
[21] Lady of Wisdom: Two, then.
[22] ¶ He fills the measure himself, with his back to her.
[23] ¶ She washes it nine times at the well and spends the last of her firewood on it. The king takes the first spoonful. Something in his mouth grinds.
[24] Heaven–Earth King: …… / Your rice has a bit of bite to it.
[25] Lady of Wisdom: ……It’s sand. / I washed it nine times.
[26] Heaven–Earth King: Who gave it to you.
[27] Lady of Wisdom: The house across the road. / I said I’d pay back two.
[28] Heaven–Earth King: Two. / One measure with sand in it, for two. / ……Eat. Eat all of it. I’m stepping out for a minute.
[29] ¶ Sumyung Jangja is counting his storehouses, which is how he prays, when the sky over the ninth one goes black at noon. The horse will not kick. The dog gets under the porch.
[30] Sumyung Jangja: Who’s there. / There’s nobody under heaven who can touch me.
[31] Heaven–Earth King: That’s why I came from above.
[32] Sumyung Jangja: ……W-what is it you want. / Rice? If it’s rice— two measures, no, ten, the whole storehouse—
[33] Heaven–Earth King: Without the sand?
[34] ¶ The floor of the ninth storehouse opens. The richest man in the world goes down through it, past the dirt and past the dark, into the place under everything where the measures are honest. He is the first one there. He will not be lonely for long.
[35] ¶ He goes back across the road. He stays until the day the calendar allows, and the morning after, he is already tying his sleeves.
[36] Lady of Wisdom: You’re going?
[37] Heaven–Earth King: Lots of work upstairs. / There are two suns, remember.
[38] Heaven–Earth King: Two sons. The first one out is Big Star, the second one Little Star. / When they turn fifteen, have them plant these.
[39] ¶ Two gourd seeds in her palm, and half of a wooden comb. The other half goes into his sleeve.
[40] Lady of Wisdom: ……Fifteen years.
[41] Heaven–Earth King: …… / Thanks for the rice.
[42] ¶ She has twins. The elder comes out quiet and looks at everything. The younger comes out already complaining. They grow up under two suns and two moons, and get asked whose sons they are in every yard in the village.
[43] [CARD Big Star: Big Star, the elder twin. He would rather be right than first.]
[44] [CARD Little Star: Little Star, the younger twin. He would rather be first.]
[45] Little Star: Mom. Who’s our father. / The other kids are at it again.
[46] Big Star: Leave it. Mom’s tired.
[47] Lady of Wisdom: ……When you’re fifteen.
[48] ── SCENE: The Gourd Vine ──
[49] ¶ At fifteen she puts the seeds in their hands and the half comb in the elder’s. They plant them by the wall at dusk. By morning the vine has gone past the roof, past the clouds, and out of sight.
[50] Lady of Wisdom: Climb. / All the way up.
[51] Little Star: What about you?
[52] Lady of Wisdom: I’ll be here. I’ll have rice on.
[53] ¶ Little Star gets to the top first and pretends he wasn’t racing. The man at the top of the vine holds out his hand without getting up.
[54] Heaven–Earth King: The comb.
[55] ¶ Big Star puts the half in his palm. The king takes the other half out of his sleeve, where it has been for fifteen years, and fits them. The teeth close.
[56] Heaven–Earth King: ……Fits.
[57] Little Star: You never came down. Not once.
[58] Heaven–Earth King: ……There were two suns.
[59] ¶ He has a thousand geun of iron melted down into two bows and two arrows, heavy enough that nobody but a son of his could draw them, and walks the boys to the edge of the sky.
[60] Heaven–Earth King: Two suns, two moons. / Two of each over your mother’s roof for fifteen years. / One each.
[61] ¶ Big Star takes the sun at noon. He breathes out once and lets go, and the second sun breaks like a plate. Its pieces scatter east and stay there as stars. At midnight Little Star draws on the second moon and hits it square, and its pieces go west.
[62] Little Star: Brother. Got it in one. / You saw?
[63] Big Star: I saw.
[64] ¶ In the morning people go out to the fields and do not fall down. That night they sleep. Nobody thanks anyone, because nobody knows who to thank.
[65] Heaven–Earth King: Done. The world’s yours. / The living side and the dead side. You two decide who takes which. / I’m not deciding. Whoever I pick always comes back to argue. / I’m resting.
[66] ── SCENE: The Contest ──
[67] ¶ They decide it the way brothers decide things. Big Star proposes riddles, which suits the one who knows the answers.
[68] Big Star: Which trees keep their leaves all their lives, and which ones drop them?
[69] Little Star: Solid ones keep them. Hollow ones drop them.
[70] Big Star: Poor little brother, don’t talk about what you don’t know. / Bamboo and reeds are hollow at every joint, and they keep their leaves.
[71] Little Star: ……Another.
[72] Big Star: Why is the grass short on the hill and long down in the hollow?
[73] Little Star: Spring rain washes the hill’s dirt down into the hollow.
[74] Big Star: Then why is the hair on your head long and the hair on your feet short?
[75] Little Star: …… / That one’s cheating.
[76] ¶ Two for two. Their father, who said he would not decide anything, leans over the edge of his rest and drops two flower seeds between them.
[77] Heaven–Earth King: Flowers. / Whoever grows the better one gets the living side. / ……That’s me done interfering.
[78] ¶ They plant them in two silver basins and sit up with them. Big Star’s flower comes up green and keeps coming, and by the third evening it has opened. Little Star’s comes up yellow and leans.
[79] Little Star: Let’s sleep, Brother. / We’ll look in the morning. See whose did better.
[80] Big Star: All right.
[81] ¶ Big Star sleeps the way honest men sleep, all the way down. Little Star lies on his side and counts his brother’s breathing up to a hundred. Then he gets up, trades the basins, and lies down again in the same shape, so his brother will wake first.
[82] Little Star: ……Brother! Wake up! / Look, it’s mine!
[83] ¶ Big Star looks at the open flower in front of his brother, the one he watered for three days. He looks at the yellow one by his own hand.
[84] Big Star: …… / Yes. Your flower did well.
[85] ¶ He gets up and brushes the soil off his knees.
[86] Big Star: Brother, countless people live in the mortal world. Among them are thieves and swindlers. To govern them well you need strength and wisdom — but above all, a true heart. So govern them, and make a beautiful, peaceful world.
[87] ¶ He is already walking toward the dark edge when he says the rest, and he does not turn round.
[88] Big Star: But, little brother. You took it with a stolen flower. / The living world will have plenty of murder, plenty of treason, plenty of thieves, and plenty of people reaching for other people’s wives and husbands. / The law down below will run clear.
[89] Little Star: ……Brother! / Brother, that’s—
[90] ¶ **Big Star** goes down. **Little Star** keeps the warm side.
[91] ¶ It goes the way his brother said, and worse, because Little Star had never thought about the parts he didn’t want. The trees still talk. So do the birds, the cattle and the stones, mostly about him. When a mother calls her son’s name at dusk a ghost answers too, and the living and the dead walk the same roads in the same clothes, and nobody can tell which is which.
[92] Little Star: Brother. / Brother, help me, just this once. / The trees talk. The ghosts answer. I can’t tell who’s a man and who’s a ghost.
[93] ¶ Big Star comes up. He scatters five measures of pine-bark powder over the world, and the trees and the birds and the cattle go quiet and have stayed quiet since. Then he hangs a scale from the sky.
[94] Big Star: Line up. / A hundred geun or more, you stay up here. / Less, you come with me.
[95] Little Star: ……And the thieves? The ones who kill people?
[96] Big Star: Those are your flower.
[97] ¶ He goes back down with the light ones following him in a long quiet line. Since then the dead weigh less than the living, the law below runs clear, and the law up here belongs to Little Star. Under Big Star, **Yumla** judges, and the measures are honest.
[98] ── SCENE: The Fire ──
[99] ¶ The fire has gone low. Gyebek sat down at some point and does not remember when.
[100] Gyebek: ……Did the brother know. That the flowers were switched.
[101] Yuri Dora: He knew.
[102] Gyebek: And he gave it up anyway.
[103] Yuri Dora: He did. And he went down. / Down there is the dead world, up here the living. There’s a flower field out at the western end, and above all of it, old Lord Hwanin. / Three Realms, all told. Tonight you only need the two.
[104] Gyebek: ……Rice with sand in it.
[105] Yuri Dora: Hm?
[106] Gyebek: Nothing.
[107] ¶ It is the first story on the island he does not inspect.
[108] ¶ **The next night Gyebek finds a roof to mend. Yuri Dora finds a ladder. One woman made this island, and she was enormous…!**

#58 Sulmun  (태초)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: halla · tone: island folklore
Logline: Before the island there is a woman, and she is enormous.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The next story is told to him on a roof, because he is on a roof, mending it, and Yuri Dora has decided that a man who will not sit down can still listen.
[1] Yuri Dora: Guests don’t mend roofs.
[2] Gyebek: I eat your rice. I mend your roof. / Then I owe nothing.
[3] Yuri Dora: And when the roof’s done?
[4] Gyebek: The wall.
[5] ¶ He drives a peg and counts it. Then, without looking down, he asks what he has wanted to ask all day.
[6] Gyebek: How far is the mainland.
[7] Yuri Dora: Two days, with a good wind. / Nobody here has a good wind for you, Turtle.
[8] Gyebek: Is there a bridge.
[9] Yuri Dora: Ha! There nearly was.
[10] Yuri Dora: One woman made this island. Sulmun.
[11] ¶ Before the island there is a woman, and she is enormous. **Sulmun**, the Great Lady. The sea comes to her knee. She scoops the seabed up in her apron and piles it in one place until it stands high enough to lean on, and that is **Mount Halla**.
[12] ¶ Some fell out on the way. The island counts three hundred and sixty-eight hills.
[13] [CARD Sulmun: Grandmother Sulmun. The sea comes to her knee, and she has opinions about the view.]
[14] [PLACE halla: The island’s spine, and a giantess’s favourite chair.]
[15] Gyebek: Was there a hole in the apron.
[16] Yuri Dora: …How did you know that?
[17] Gyebek: You said there are three hundred and sixty-eight hills. / If it were poured in one place there would be one.
[18] ¶ Yuri Dora looks at him for a while.
[19] Yuri Dora: You do not listen to a story. You inspect it.
[20] Gyebek: …Yes.
[21] ¶ She had five hundred sons. In a famine she set a cauldron of porridge to boil for them, and slipped, and did not come out. The sons ate. It was the best they had ever tasted, and they said so, and then the youngest reached the bottom and found his mother’s bones.
[22] ¶ The hammering stops.
[23] Gyebek: …They said it was good.
[24] Yuri Dora: The best they ever had.
[25] Gyebek: It was not their fault that it was good.
[26] Yuri Dora: No. That’s why the youngest walked into the sea.
[27] ¶ The youngest walked into the sea and would not turn round, and stands there yet as a single rock off the shore. The other four hundred and ninety-nine went up the mountain and wept until they were stone. You can go and count them. Nobody has ever got the same number twice.
[28] Gyebek: I will count them.
[29] Yuri Dora: Everybody says that.
[30] ¶ He counts them on his first free morning and gets four hundred and ninety-eight. He goes back the next morning to find the one he missed.
[31] ❝QUOTE (Chogamje (초감제), Nalgwa-guk-seomgim, recited by Gang Sun-seon (강순선), recorded by Heo Nam-chun, Gang Jeong-sik, Gang So-jeon and Song Jeong-hui, 2009 — Tapdong Yeongdeung-gut, Jeju City (Hanguk Gubimunhak Daegye, rev. ed.)): Five hundred shrines before that mountain, five hundred temples before this one. Five hundred generals, five hundred teachers. One valley short, so it is an island that could raise no king, no tiger, no bear.❞
[32] Yuri Dora: So the island had stone sons, and no bridge. She meant to fix that.
[33] ¶ She asked the islanders for one thing: clothes her size, a hundred rolls of silk, and she would lay a bridge to the mainland. They found ninety-nine. The collar was never finished. Neither was the bridge.
[34] Gyebek: They were one roll short.
[35] Yuri Dora: They were.
[36] Gyebek: …That is the worst amount to be short by.
[37] ¶ He finishes the roof by feel after dark. He comes down with one peg left over, and goes back up to find the hole it belongs in.
[38] ¶ In the morning he cuts a notch in the beam by the door. Nine hundred and sixty.
[39] ¶ **Three princes climb out of the ground. “Not from an egg,” the island insists. Then a box drifts in from the sea…!**

=================================================================
#59 Three Princes  (태초)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: samseonghyeol · tone: island folklore
Logline: Three princes climb out of a hole in the ground. A chest sealed with purple clay is drifting toward their beach.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Half the kingdoms on the mainland have a first king who hatched from an egg. Tamla is proud to say its kings climbed out of a hole.
[1] [DIAGRAM tamla-princes Three Princes · 삼성혈 — Three divine princes rise from Samseonghyeol and divide the orange island.]
[2] ── SCENE: The Diver ──
[3] ¶ Ordinary Tamla does not play the mainland’s endless status games. A diver offers **Gyebek** grilled fish before she asks which Baekje office ruined him. Since the arrow he has not eaten food he did not watch being cooked. So he watches. She turns the fish; he watches the fish. She laughs at him and turns it slower. Kindness here is not strategy. It takes him most of a year to believe that.
[4] The Divers: Eat. / You look like a man who was promoted by being useful and punished for the same crime. That joke is how Little Star runs the living world.
[5] Gyebek: …That is an exact sentence.
[6] The Divers: We have those. We just don’t put them on banners.
[7] Gyebek: Why do you feed me. / I am Baekje’s prisoner.
[8] The Divers: You’re the island’s guest. / This island came out of a hole in the ground, Turtle. It doesn’t ask whose son you are.
[9] ¶ Long after the Great Lady’s stone sons, three divine princes climb out of a hole in the ground. Nobody hatches. They each shoot an arrow and rule wherever it lands. One day a box drifts from the East Sea, with a messenger and three princesses inside. They marry the three princesses at a pond. The box also holds calves, foals and the five grains. That is how Tamla learns to farm, and how it learns that anything worth having arrives by sea in a container.
[10] Gyebek: And Baekje’s prisoners.
[11] The Divers: Those came later. Ask the king.
[12] ── SCENE: Baekjuto and Socheon-guk ──
[13] ¶ Told some evenings later, while he is stacking oranges badly, which Yuri Dora treats as invitation.
[14] Gyebek: Do they go home. / The men Baekje sends here.
[15] Yuri Dora: Some. Let me tell you about one whose own parents threw him out.
[16] Yuri Dora: The hunting god married the farming goddess. / She gave him an ox to plough with—
[17] Gyebek: He ate it.
[18] Yuri Dora: …Have you heard this one?
[19] Gyebek: No. But he is a hunter.
[20] [CARD Baekjuto: A farming goddess who crossed the sea to find a husband. She is about to find one.]
[21] Baekjuto: You ate the ox. The one I gave you to plough with. The _whole_ ox?
[22] [CARD Socheon-guk: The hunt god. A big appetite. Bigger than you’re thinking.]
[23] Socheon-guk: …I also ate someone else’s.
[24] ¶ They separated. It is the first divorce in the record, the grounds are livestock, and the islanders tell it as a comedy because it is one.
[25] ¶ Their son kicked his father in the chest at three years old. So they put the boy in an iron chest, locked it, and set it on the water.
[26] ¶ It drifted for years and washed up in a foreign country, and the boy came out of it a warrior, and won that country’s wars, and married its princess. And then he came home.
[27] Gyebek: …Tell that part again.
[28] Yuri Dora: Which part.
[29] Gyebek: The part where he comes home.
[30] Yuri Dora: He came home and became the god of his own land. / The god the ones who threw him out have to bow to.
[31] Gyebek: How long was he in the chest.
[32] Yuri Dora: Years.
[33] Gyebek: How many.
[34] Yuri Dora: The story doesn’t say.
[35] Gyebek: …It should.
[36] ¶ On the way back he says the count out loud, which he has never done in front of anyone. Nine hundred and twelve. Yuri Dora hears it and, for once, says nothing.
[37] ¶ **“Tomorrow’s isn’t a kind one, Turtle.” A serpent in a cave. A woman from the rock. A man who looks back…!**

#60 Stone Lady  (태초)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: halla · tone: island folklore
Logline: Sanbangduk came down out of the rock to love a poor man. The island remembers how that went.
=================================================================
[0] Yuri Dora: Today’s is not a kind one.
[1] Gyebek: That is acceptable.
[2] ¶ A year has gone. He still walks to the shore every dawn and looks at the sea, the same way, for the same count. Five hundred and ninety-six.
[3] Yuri Dora: You looked at the sea again.
[4] Gyebek: Every morning.
[5] Yuri Dora: Then you get the one about looking back.
[6] ¶ There is the serpent in the cave at Gimnyeong that took a girl a year until a young magistrate went in and killed it, and was told on the way out not to look back, and looked back.
[7] Gyebek: Why did he look back.
[8] Yuri Dora: To check that he had won.
[9] Gyebek: I will not look back.
[10] Yuri Dora: You look back every morning, Turtle. At the sea.
[11] Gyebek: That is not back. / That is Sabi.
[12] ── SCENE: Sanbangdeok ──
[13] ¶ There is **Sanbangduk**, who came down out of the rock to love a poor man.
[14] [CARD Sanbangduk: A goddess who stepped out of the Sanbang cliff to see the world. The world noticed.]
[15] Sanbangduk: I came out of the rock… / and when I hold your hand I don’t feel like stone.
[16] The Husband: Then don’t let go. / Whatever the official says.
[17] ¶ Then an official on a tax round sees her at the spring.
[18] The Official: A woman out of the rock belongs to the government. / Like the rock.
[19] The Husband: She belongs to nobody. She picked a hut.
[20] ¶ Poor men always owe something somewhere, and the official finds it. Then the official has the husband killed to take her.
[21] Sanbangduk: You wanted me because I wasn’t stone. / Look again.
[22] ¶ She walks back into the cliff. The spring inside it has not stopped since.
[23] Gyebek: She went back into the rock. / …The rock did not lie to her.
[24] Gyebek: Do all the stories on this island end badly.
[25] Yuri Dora: No. They all end as **stone**. / That’s not the same as badly. Stone stays.
[26] ── SCENE: Gameunjang ──
[27] ¶ Told at a well, while he is fixing the rope.
[28] Gyebek: The men Baekje sends here. / Were any of them right.
[29] Yuri Dora: Right about what?
[30] Gyebek: Anything.
[31] Yuri Dora: Ha. Here’s a girl who was right about one thing. It went badly for her family.
[32] Yuri Dora: A rich man had three daughters. He asked them whose luck they lived on.
[33] Yuri Dora: The elder two said his. The youngest said her own navel-string. / So she was thrown out.
[34] ❝QUOTE (Samgong Bonpuri (삼공본풀이) recited by Jeong Tae-jin (정태진), recorded by Gang Jeong-sik, Gang So-jeon and Song Jeong-hui, 2011 — Sanggari, Aewol-eup (Hanguk Gubimunhak Daegye, rev. ed.)): “By whose grace did you come into the world?” “First, heaven’s. Second, earth’s. Third, Father’s. Fourth, Mother’s — but really, the line drawn under Mother’s navel.”❞
[35] Gyebek: If she had lied she could have stayed.
[36] Yuri Dora: …Yes. She could have.
[37] ¶ She walked until she found three brothers digging yams and married the youngest, the only one who greeted her. In the spoil he had been throwing away as stones, she found gold.
[38] ¶ Her parents lost everything and went blind. Years later she held a beggars’ feast that lasted three days, and served two old blind beggars herself, and said her name, and their eyes opened.
[39] Gyebek: …So the child they threw away was the luck.
[40] Yuri Dora: No. The luck was always hers. / It was the ones who threw her out who went blind.
[41] ¶ He does not answer that one. He finishes the rope, and tests it eleven times.
[42] ¶ **Heaven sends for a man to keep its flower field. He leaves his pregnant wife to wait. He forgets to say how long…!**

#61 Gardener  (태초)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: western_flower_field · tone: island folklore
Logline: At the far end of the west, where the maps run out, there is a field of flowers that put the dead back together.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Told in the orange grove, in the hour after the picking, when Gyebek has finally been persuaded to sit on a basket.
[1] ¶ The baskets are for the tribute boat. It leaves for Sabi in the morning, full of oranges and empty of him.
[2] Gyebek: Can the boat carry a word.
[3] Yuri Dora: To your king?
[4] ¶ He does not answer, which is new.
[5] Yuri Dora: Hm. Then sit. Here’s one about a man who left somebody waiting.
[6] Yuri Dora: There was a man called Sara Doryeong. Heaven sent for him to keep its flower field in the west. / His wife was carrying. She couldn’t walk as fast as heaven wanted, so he left her at a rich man’s house to wait.
[7] Gyebek: How long was she to wait.
[8] Yuri Dora: He didn’t say. / That’s the first mistake. Count it if you like.
[9] ¶ The rich man wanted her. She said no, and went on saying no for fifteen years, through every kind of work a rich man can find for a servant who says no. Her son was born in that house and grew up a servant in it. His name was **Hallakgungi**.
[10] [CARD Hallakgungi: Hallakgungi. Born a servant, and he means to find his father.]
[11] Yuri Dora: When he was old enough she told him where his father was. He went west that night. / And the rich man, when he found the boy gone, killed the mother instead and threw her into a bamboo grove.
[12] Gyebek: …She knew he would.
[13] Yuri Dora: She knew. / She told him anyway.
[14] ¶ Hallakgungi found the flower field at the far end of the west, where the living maps run out, and his father at the gate of it. Sara Doryeong took him down the rows. Here, the flowers that put back bone, and flesh, and blood, and breath, and the soul last of all. Over there, the flowers that laugh a man to death, and the ones that make a house fight itself, and at the end of the row the one that ends a line altogether.
[15] Gyebek: Which did he take.
[16] Yuri Dora: Both rows. / He went back to that rich man’s house and held a little party. Laughing flower, fighting flower, and the last one. Then he went to the bamboo grove and found his mother’s bones, and put her back together in order. Bone, flesh, blood, breath, soul.
[17] Gyebek: In order. / …Good.
[18] ¶ Afterwards the son took the flower field over from his father and keeps it still. The island calls him the Gardener when it does not want to say his name, which is most of the time. The flowers that bring you back and the flowers that end you grow in the same rows, and he is the only one who knows which is which in the dark.
[19] Gyebek: Did the father go home with them.
[20] Yuri Dora: No. He kept the gate till the boy was ready for it. / …You ask the right questions in the wrong places, Turtle.
[21] Gyebek: I did not say either.
[22] Yuri Dora: Say what?
[23] Gyebek: How long. / My wife asked at the berth. I said I did not know.
[24] ¶ Yuri Dora puts down his orange.
[25] Yuri Dora: You have a wife.
[26] Gyebek: And a son. And a daughter.
[27] Yuri Dora: A whole year of evenings, and you never said.
[28] Gyebek: You did not ask.
[29] Yuri Dora: ……So. The word on the boat.
[30] Gyebek: Tell her three hundred and forty-one days. / Then His Majesty can sign. Then he sends for me.
[31] ¶ It is the first number he has ever given her. It is the king’s.
[32] ── SCENE: Jacheongbi ──
[33] ¶ Told in the rain, in a doorway, which is the only time anyone gets him to stand still.
[34] Yuri Dora: Jacheongbi wanted to study beside a boy from the sky. / Women were not allowed in the room, so she cut her hair and put on a man’s clothes.
[35] [CARD Jacheongbi: Jacheongbi. Disguise, scholarship, and not one ounce of patience.]
[36] Gyebek: Did she break the rule.
[37] Yuri Dora: No. The rule never said a woman could not wear a man’s clothes.
[38] Gyebek: …Ah.
[39] ¶ Three years at the same desk. She beat him at everything and let him believe it was close. On the last night at the parting stream she washed upstream of him and told him to look.
[40] Jacheongbi: Three years at the same table — eating, sleeping, reading — and you notice _now_?
[41] [CARD Mun Doryeong: A boy from the sky, sent down to study. Very good at books, very bad at noticing things.]
[42] Mun Doryeong: …I had no eyes.
[43] Jacheongbi: You have them now. / …Will you only look? / After three years of holding back.
[44] Mun Doryeong: I was not holding back. / I did not know. / Now that I do… my breath is rough.
[45] Jacheongbi: Then stay rough. / Touch my hair. / The hair I cut short for you.
[46] ¶ Heaven does not care for that sort of marriage. They kill him for it, and send his body down the parting stream, past her.
[47] Jacheongbi: You noticed me late. / You don’t get to leave early.
[48] ¶ So she walks west, past every gate, into the Western Flower Field.
[49] [PLACE western_flower_field: Every flower here does something. Ask before you pick.]
[50] Hallakgungi: Father retired. / This gate answers to Hallakgungi now. / What are you looking for.
[51] Jacheongbi: The resurrection flower. / The one that puts bones back together.
[52] Hallakgungi: Don’t touch the stem wrong. / Five — bone, flesh, blood, breath, soul. / Pick them out of order and even the living wilt.
[53] Jacheongbi: I’ll pick them in order.
[54] ¶ She picks the five flowers in order and puts him back together bone by bone. Bone, flesh, blood, breath, soul. He sits up on the bank like a man woken too early.
[55] Mun Doryeong: …How long was I gone.
[56] Jacheongbi: Long enough. Don’t do it again.
[57] ¶ Then she brings the five grains down to Tamla, because a woman who has been to the end of the west does not come home empty-handed.
[58] Gyebek: …Can the dead be fetched back.
[59] Yuri Dora: In stories.
[60] Gyebek: …I see.
[61] ¶ **The island keeps one story for last. It is about the one who comes for you, and the crow that lost his book…!**

=================================================================
#62 Kangrim  (태초)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · tone: psychopomp ritual
Logline: A diver drowns, and the island tells its last story: the strongman who went down alive to arrest the judge of the dead, and the crow that lost the book of everyone’s hour.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ On this island, a death gets a fire on the shore and one story.
[1] ¶ This winter it is the diver who grilled his fish. She went down at the third rock and did not come up. Gyebek was in the water with the others until dark, counting other people’s breaths.
[2] Gyebek: She was twenty-six. / Her mother is on the shore.
[3] Yuri Dora: She is.
[4] Gyebek: That is the wrong order.
[5] Yuri Dora: It is. Sit, Turtle. The island keeps one story for last, and this is why.
[6] Yuri Dora: Now the last one. / Kangrim. / Heaven did not send him.
[7] ¶ A rich couple killed three brothers for their silk and sank them in a pond. The brothers came back, and died again, and no living court could try a case like that. So the magistrate, a man called Gimchi, sent his strongest man down to fetch the judge of the dead.
[8] Gyebek: How did they come back.
[9] Yuri Dora: Three flowers on the water. Three beads. Three sons. Don’t ask, that part takes a whole night. / And yes, Gimchi. Don’t laugh. He was a serious man.
[10] Gyebek: I was not going to laugh.
[11] Gyebek: …He sent a living man to arrest the judge of the dead.
[12] Yuri Dora: He did.
[13] ── SCENE: The Road Down ──
[14] ¶ His wife kept the gate-god and the kitchen-god fed, so they put him on the road. At the last pond he shut his eyes and jumped, and stood up at the underworld gate. Someone was already walking that road with a red book. Haewonmek, the oldest fetch there is. Kangrim asked the way. Haewonmek pointed, and kept walking. Kangrim waited, and addressed King Yumla with court courtesy.
[15] Kangrim: Your Majesty. The living court requests you. / There is a case. Living law cannot close it.
[16] [CARD Yumla: The judge of the dead. Every ledger in the dark ends on his desk.]
[17] Yumla: Go home. / I will come at the hour I name.
[18] ¶ He came. The pond dried. The bones came up. The three brothers went home to their parents. The couple who had killed them did not. **Yumla** keeps the sentence. Then he turned to the magistrate and asked to borrow the man who had fetched him.
[19] Yumla: Lend me that man. I still have errands.
[20] Yuri Dora: The magistrate refused. He did not believe in a soul. / So they split him. The magistrate kept the body. Yumla took the soul.
[21] ¶ That is how Kangrim died upstairs and woke as a fetch of the dead. The living official kept the half he could see. Death kept the other half.
[22] Gyebek: …They divided a man.
[23] Yuri Dora: They both wanted him.
[24] ¶ Yumla then put in his hands a ledger that told each living person their hour — eighty, and in order, the old before the young. On the way down Kangrim trusted it to a crow. The crow set the book on a wall to eat at a slaughter-field. A snake swallowed the writing. Caught, the crow cried a new rule so the blame would not sit on one bird: parents after children, children after parents. Since then the hour does not come in a just order.
[25] ❝QUOTE (Chasa Bonpuri (차사본풀이) recited by Go Yeon-ok (고연옥), recorded by Gang Jeong-sik, Gang So-jeon and Song Jeong-hui, 2011 — Sanggari, Aewol-eup; sung as Cheseo Bonpuri (체서본풀이) (Hanguk Gubimunhak Daegye, rev. ed.)): “Give me the red writ. When it’s the old one’s turn, let the child come. When it’s the child’s turn, let the old one come. I’ll bring them back like water running uphill, out of order.”❞
[26] ¶ One errand was left: a man who had dodged death for three thousand years. Kangrim sat in a stream washing charcoal until the old man stopped to laugh at him, and took him by the sleeve. Only then did Yumla seat him as the one who comes for everyone else. That is why he asks a question at the threshold. Not for the sentence — Yumla keeps the sentence. A scrambled list still deserves accurate last words.
[27] Kangrim: I do not punish. / I collect — for His Majesty. / Since the list was scrambled, nobody knows the hour until I am already in the room.
[28] Gyebek: …Then a man can die before his king, and the book still opens.
[29] Yuri Dora: The book went wrong on the road. The walk did not. / That is the key.
[30] Gyebek: Then she gets a question.
[31] Yuri Dora: She gets a question. And she gets to answer it.
[32] ¶ Walking home, he says the count to the dark. Twelve. In twelve days the king’s rite ends, and the tribute boat is already in Sabi.
[33] ¶ **In spring the tribute boat comes back from Sabi with news of the king. Gyebek has one question for it…!**

#63 Tribute  (498)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · tone: island folklore chronicle
Logline: The tribute boat comes home from Sabi with the king’s news. None of it has Gyebek’s name in it.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The tribute boat comes home light. The oranges stayed in Sabi. The news did not.
[1] ¶ Gyebek is on the sand before the sail has a shape. The captain holds a Yunbi contract and has been told not to talk to him. He talks anyway. It is a long way to sail with a thing like that in your mouth.
[2] The Captain: The rite is over, General. Done at the new year. / His Majesty calls the Assembly on the first of the month. All eight houses.
[3] Gyebek: Did he send for me.
[4] The Captain: …… / Nobody said your name, General.
[5] Gyebek: Did anyone say it.
[6] The Captain: No. / …Your wife came to the berth when we docked. She said to tell you— / the boy counts too.
[7] ¶ Gyebek thanks him exactly once. He walks up the beach to the beam by the door, where the notches have run out. Nothing. He has never had a number end on him before.
[8] ── SCENE: The Forgotten Oranges ──
[9] Gyebek: Why does your island keep Baekje’s men. / You owe Baekje nothing.
[10] Yuri Dora: Owe nothing? Ha. Once, long ago, we forgot the oranges.
[11] ¶ One year, long ago, Tamla stops sending tribute. Rebellion would at least have been legible. This is closer to forgetting, which a large kingdom finds harder to forgive.
[12] ¶ Baekje’s king marches an army to the southern harbour and stops. He lets the news cross the water on its own. It gets there faster than he would have.
[13] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 26, Baekje Annals — King Dongseong, yr. 20 (498), eighth month): Eighth month. Because Tamla had not sent its tribute, the king went out to punish it himself and got as far as Mujin Province. Tamla heard, sent envoys to beg pardon, and he stopped.❞
[14] Yuri Dora: See what he did? He marched to the harbour, and stopped. / He didn’t want to cross. He wanted us to know he could.
[15] ¶ Tamla apologises. Baekje accepts. Nobody is killed, everybody is satisfied, and the oranges resume. For a hundred and fifty years, that is the whole relationship.
[16] ¶ So when Baekje needs somewhere to put a man it cannot kill, there is an island, and the island owes it a favour.
[17] Gyebek: His Majesty will cross. / After the Assembly.
[18] Yuri Dora: Turtle. A king who marches to the harbour and stops is telling you something.
[19] Gyebek: His Majesty has not marched to the harbour. / So he has not stopped.
[20] ¶ Yuri Dora opens his mouth, and shuts it. There is no answer to that. There is only the next morning.
[21] ¶ He has run out of days to count. So at dawn he goes down to the black rock and starts counting something else.
[22] ── SCENE: Black Rock ──
[23] ¶ He trains at the same hour on the same slab of lava on the eastern shore, and when the tide takes that slab he waits for the tide rather than use another one.
[24] Yuri Dora: The next rock is the same.
[25] Gyebek: It is not the same.
[26] ¶ The rock is porous and cruel and nothing like a drill ground. You cannot plant a foot on it twice in the same place. Two seasons of it and he no longer needs to know where his feet are.
[27] The Divers: You don’t hold the breath. You push it out with singing.
[28] Gyebek: …I cannot sing.
[29] The Divers: Nobody cannot. There are only people who don’t.
[30] ¶ The village children learn the count of his drills before they learn his name, and stand on the rocks doing it badly behind him, and he does not once turn round to stop them, because stopping would be an interruption and he does not interrupt.
[31] [MORAL the warning: A man who cannot vary anything will be unbeatable on the ground he chose, and helpless on any other. Give him the choosing.]
[32] ── SCENE: Five Thousand ──
[33] ¶ He is asked, once, why he counts everything, and he answers honestly, which is the only way he has ever answered anything.
[34] Gyebek: Numbers do not lie to me.
[35] Yuri Dora: And people do?
[36] Gyebek: People are not trying to. / I simply do not follow them. / I have never learned to read a face.
[37] Yuri Dora: Then how did you survive twenty years at a court?
[38] Gyebek: I trusted one man.
[39] ¶ The island considers this the saddest sentence anybody has said on it, and nobody explains to him why they have all gone quiet, and he does not ask, because he has not noticed.
[40] ?: (Tamla fisher, laughing) / Hundred-Victories, they call him on the mainland — and here he counts oranges like they might desert.
[41] ¶ He drills in units of five hundred. One day he will take ten of those units to a field and leave the rest behind. The count is already in his mouth.
[42] ¶ That night he cuts a new notch at the other end of the beam. One. If the king sends, he will be ready. If the king does not send, he will be ready.
[43] ¶ **Meanwhile, in Sabi, Euija calls the Assembly. He has a smile, a speech, and a proclamation printed before anyone sat down…!**

=================================================================
#64 Coup  (657 February)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: sabi · tone: coup satire — martial law as theatre
Logline: He calls the assembly the way a gambler calls a final hand.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ He calls the assembly the way a gambler calls a final hand — smiling, sleeves perfect, already knowing which tiles he slipped into the set.
[1] [MAP 657: ]
[2] ¶ Mourning ends at dawn. By breakfast **Euija** has called the Ministers’ Assembly to the Rock of Politics. The rock is dry. Someone forgot the brine, or remembered it and chose not to.
[3] King Euija: Beloved people. / As Eraha, I appeal to you with a heart that spits blood. / To eradicate in one stroke the shameless pro-Tang anti-state forces that plunder our people’s freedom and happiness — / I hereby declare emergency martial law.
[4] ¶ Somebody coughs. Nobody looks at the rock. On the Satek bench a young man leans to his elder and whispers, loud enough to carry two benches over.
[5] Satek Chunbok: King Onjo preserve us — he’s lost his mind… / Also he printed the proclamation before the session. I can smell the ink. / The characters for “in one stroke” are still wet.
[6] King Euija: There may be some inconveniences for the good people who have followed the lawful order of this country. / We will strive to minimize such inconveniences. / I place my trust solely in you. / Please trust me.
[7] Minister Satek: Majesty. For how long?
[8] King Euija: This is temporary. / Temporary is how permanent things begin when you are afraid to say permanent.
[9] ¶ Then he unrolls a second scroll — shorter, denser, the kind of law that fits on one sheet because the power is in what it erases. The clerks name it before he does: the Law to Remedy the Distress of the People and the Country.
[10] King Euija: Laws of Baekje may also be enacted by the Eraha’s command. / Such laws may deviate from old custom — insofar as the Assembly as such is not abolished. / The existence of the Assembly is not endangered. The Premier’s chair remains undisturbed.
[11] Minister Satek: Your Majesty. That is… a law for emptying the Assembly. / It keeps the name. It changes the people.
[12] King Euija: If the name remains, the country remains. / If the people remain, the people eat the country. / May you now choose for yourselves — peace, or war.
[13] ¶ Nobody chooses war out loud. Choosing peace means raising a sleeve for the scroll, and for a long moment nobody does that either. Then a sleeve goes up on the Satek bench. It belongs to **Satek Chunbok**, the young man who was whispering about wet ink.
[14] Minister Satek: Chunbok. Put your arm down.
[15] Satek Chunbok: As my lord well knows, His Majesty asked for peace or war. / I am choosing peace.
[16] ¶ The old men try to rally, Satek calling in four generations of favors. Too late. The other houses, the ones Satek kept out of the light for a century, raise their sleeves one after another, delighted. Some are already paid. Some are already afraid. Some are the king’s own sons, waiting in the corridor.
[17] ¶ A face-off only works if you know your opponent’s style, and Euija has spent twenty years teaching them his. They lined up for a duel. He had already changed who was sitting.
[18] ¶ Euija names forty-one of his own sons to the Assembly, firing every single existing member. Eight houses spent four generations sharpening tricks on each other. Marriages. Roads. Clerks planted in rival counting-rooms. In one morning the king clears the board. He simply changes the pieces. By noon nobody has an answer.
[19] [DIAGRAM ministers-assembly:purged The Rock of Politics, after · 정사암, 그 후 — The same benches. Every one of them a son.]
[20] ¶ **Satek Chunbok** is named Premier. His own clan watches him walk to the chair. The Enabling Law did not abolish the chair. It only changed who sits in it.
[21] [CARD Satek Chunbok — Premier of Baekje: A Satek in the Satek chair, sitting for the king.]
[22] ¶ Forty-one sons need forty-one seats. None goes to the Ye family. They have held Bear Fortress for four generations and never once been asked to court. Ye Sikjin reads the list at home, twice. Then he puts it in a drawer.
[23] [PLACE ungjin: Four generations of the Ye family, and not one invitation.]
[24] ¶ Then he hands out the quiet money that really runs Baekje. Harbour warehouses. River pilot fees. The stamp a ship needs before it sails east. The martial law was the noise. The stamps are what change.
[25] ¶ He cannot do what Yeon did. Baekje would not forgive it, and more to the point, he would not. He does not need a banquet. He needs a majority that looks like kinship.
[26] ── SCENE: That Night ──
[27] ¶ That night he writes one letter himself, with no clerk in the room. It is short, because the man it is for cannot read. A boatman will have to say it to him aloud.
[28] King Euija: Tamla. The fastest boat in the harbour. / Tonight, Chunbok. Before the old men finish counting what they lost.
[29] Satek Chunbok: Your Majesty… as Your Majesty well knows, the houses are counting tonight. / If a boat leaves for Tamla before the benches are cold, they will read it as war. / Let them get used to losing first. A month. Then send for him.
[30] King Euija: …A month. / Fine. A month. He’s good at waiting. He counts.
[31] ¶ He folds the letter into his sleeve. It will stay there a good deal longer than a month.
[32] The Court Maids: Your Majesty. How many did you dismiss today? / …And how many of us will you keep.
[33] King Euija: All of them. / You… I keep.
[34] The Court Maids: …How frightening. / And yet — that kind of Majesty… feels nearer.
[35] King Euija: …What was your name again.
[36] The Court Maids: I don’t have one yet. / Make me one tonight. / As you did for General Gyebek — take your time.
[37] ¶ Eleven of them by morning.
[38] ¶ Months later, the new Premier is in Chang’an, talking too much. A spy who learns his trade that well rarely works for only one house.
[39] ── SCENE: Chang’an ──
[40] The Third Emperor: So… Baekje? What of Baekje—
[41] Satek Chunbok: Do not trouble yourself over Baekje.
[42] The Third Emperor: ?
[43] Satek Chunbok: Baekje will fall on its own. / Where blood ties are strong, the state grows weak. / The Baekje clans love a family feud — they will envy each other into ruin.
[44] The Third Emperor: Then why am I needed at all?
[45] Satek Chunbok: However weak it is, it still needs one shock. / Say the Tang army is coming — the rumour alone will tip the country’s spirit.
[46] ¶ **He beat eight houses in one morning. Now he can’t sleep. In his dreams, somebody keeps counting…?**

#65 Descent  (657 September)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: sabi · tone: clan face-off (shonen)
Logline: Eight grudges, forty-one sons, and not one loyalty he didn’t create by decree.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: Nightmares ──
[1] ¶ He starts dreaming about the Rock of Politics. In the dream it is dry, and he is rubbing it with brine, and the brine will not stay. Every time he lifts the cloth the stone is dry again, and the eight elders are standing round it waiting for it to sweat.
[2] ¶ Some nights it is the white deer, come back out of the dark it was kept in, and too big for the hunting ground. Some nights it is a boat on the water with a man sitting very straight in the stern, not rowing, counting.
[3] King Euija: (waking, to the dark) Who’s counting? / …Who’s there. Light. Somebody bring a light!
[4] The Court Maids: Majesty. It’s only us. / …You were saying numbers again.
[5] King Euija: Wine. / No. Don’t water it. I can tell when you water it.
[6] ── SCENE: The Hall ──
[7] ¶ The first man to say the obvious thing out loud is **Heungsu**. He says it smiling, the way he says everything.
[8] Heungsu: The Diamond Sutra says every made thing is like a dream, Majesty. A dewdrop. A flash of lightning. / Your new Assembly is a made thing.
[9] King Euija: Heungsu. Is this a sermon or a memorial?
[10] Heungsu: Both, Majesty. The sermon is free. / Bring the Satek and Yunbi men back to the benches before winter. If Silla comes, it comes over Tanhyeon. If Tang comes—
[11] King Euija: —it comes up the river. Yes. I can read a map. / You have a lovely voice, Heungsu. Gomamiji has nobody to hear it. Go and read them sutras.
[12] ¶ Euija calls it a temporary posting. The court knows better. The paper names a county far to the south: packed earth, a magistrate’s hut, and a long way from anyone who matters.
[13] ── SCENE: Gomamiji ──
[14] ¶ Gomamiji is a posting, not a retirement. He sits on the threshold until the dust on the hem looks like the hem. His office sword hangs on the doorpost. Nobody from Sabi writes.
[15] ── SCENE: The Banquet Hall ──
[16] ¶ He stops holding court. The wine comes earlier each day, and then it stops being tied to the day at all.
[17] ¶ Hundreds, by now. Nobody keeps the roll. They no longer have separate duties — only who pours, who steadies his wrist, who is still there when the wine runs out, and who is bold enough to speak while his mouth is busy elsewhere.
[18] ¶ The hems keep time better than the roll. A pour, a step, a kneel — the long court silk opens, and he watches that before he watches the wine.
[19] ¶ The feast is no longer a feast. The stories say three thousand. The room is not that. It is still too many, a harem so packed the lamp never finds a wall. Robes open early. The maids show him their bodies the way other courts show tribute, and he studies them the way he once studied a map.
[20] ¶ He is half-undressed by the second jar and does not bother to hide what the wine has done to him. They climb into his lap two at a time. They hike the silk and laugh when he looks. They toast until the lamps blur. On rainy nights the party spills out onto the night veranda, and he follows a hip down the night corridor as if it were the last order anyone will ever give him.
[21] ¶ Here is what the lamps do not show. The headband is gone, and nobody tells him to put it back on. The prince who could read a room in one glance cannot read past the next fold of silk. Every one of them flatters him. He knows it, and he likes knowing it. It is the only sum left in Sabi that always comes out in his favour.
[22] The Court Maids: Your Majesty. You said that yesterday, and again today. / …With the same breath on us. / The same teeth… at our collarbones.
[23] King Euija: Was it good? / Or… was it a good night.
[24] The Court Maids: …It was, yesterday. / The body still remembers. / Even if Your Majesty says stop… the hips answer first.
[25] The Court Maids: Your Majesty. Tell us about when you were young. / Before you… undo anything. / No — / While you undo it. / One word per knot.
[26] King Euija: …What is it you want to know.
[27] The Court Maids: They say you have more than fifty sons. / Samsin must keep a whole ledger just for Your Majesty. The kitchens have a wager going on how. / Nightly.
[28] King Euija: …That was the thirtieth Eraha. My father.
[29] The Court Maids: Ah. Then Your Majesty still has room to work with. / We can testify to it.
[30] The Court Maids: We knew already, in fairness. / Asking was only manners.
[31] ¶ He laughs for the first time in four months. It is the last recorded instance.
[32] ¶ Somewhere in the third year he stops going out to the hall, and some time after that they stop sending for him. The distance between those two things is the rest of the reign.
[33] ¶ Every season Chunbok asks the same question, in front of witnesses, the way a careful man pays a small tax. It buys him a name for loyalty. He already knows the answer.
[34] Satek Chunbok: Your Majesty…
[35] Satek Chunbok: Would it not be best to bring back General Gyebek?
[36] ¶ The letter is still in the king’s sleeve. It has gone soft at the folds.
[37] King Euija: That… who? / You there! Bring more wine!
[38] Baekje: Ahh~~ over here, Your Majesty~~
[39] The Court Maids: Your Majesty. The ministers are waiting outside.
[40] King Euija: …Let them wait.
[41] The Court Maids: Until when?
[42] King Euija: …
[43] ¶ He does not answer. After a while the question stops being asked, and after a while longer the ministers stop coming to the door. He notices none of it, and it is the first thing in his life he has not arranged on purpose.
[44] ¶ **Sungchung** comes while the wine is still being poured. He does not wait for a gap. He is the councillor who used to read the tides for the king, and he still wears his office sword as if there were an office.
[45] Sungchung: Your Majesty. Open court. Today.
[46] King Euija: We opened it. / With the cup.
[47] Sungchung: There is a tide. / If you miss it—
[48] ¶ He does not finish. The king is already on his feet.
[49] King Euija: Take his belt. / He wants open court? Give him a room where he can talk all day.
[50] ¶ The belt comes off in the aisle, and his rank goes with it. The guards walk him to a cell. After that, nobody else tries to speak.
[51] ── SCENE: The Cell ──
[52] ¶ **Sungchung** starves in a cell within earshot of the feast. His office sword hangs on the post outside. With the last of his ink he writes the king one page.
[53] ¶ In the cell where he starved, Kangrim reads his name three times — Sungchung. Sungchung. Sungchung. — loud enough for the feast next door to hear, or not hear.
[54] Kangrim: Councillor Sungchung. / You chose the cell over silence. Was that loyalty to the king — or loyalty to being right?
[55] Sungchung: …Being right is the only loyalty left when a king stops listening. / The paper is for him. Not for you.
[56] Kangrim: I will keep the minutes. Walk.
[57] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 16, dying memorial of Seongchung; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 384): A loyal servant does not forget his king even in death, so let me say one thing and die. I have always watched the times and studied their changes, and there will surely be war. Whoever uses soldiers must choose his ground with care: take the upper stream and draw the enemy to you, and you can keep the country whole. If foreign soldiers come, do not let them cross Chimhyeon by land, and do not let their ships into the banks of Final Ford. Hold the narrow, difficult places, and stop them there.❞
[58] ¶ The page reaches the banquet hall folded inside a guard’s glove. The king reads the first line. Then he sets it under a wine jar, and does not take it in.
[59] ¶ **Foxes in the Assembly. Toads in the treetops. A river running red. Nine signs, and a king who swears he doesn’t believe in signs…!**

#66 Nine Omens  (659)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: sabi · tone: omen dread
Logline: Every omen is real, in the sense that people saw it. That was always the only sense that mattered.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Every one of the nine signs is real, in the sense that people saw it. That was always the only sense that mattered, and the man who taught Baekje so is about to find out how much he meant it.
[1] ¶ Foxes walk into the Assembly hall in a pack, and a white one sits down on the Premier’s desk. A hen mates with a sparrow. A dead fish as long as a boat washes up on the river. Then a dead woman, longer than the fish.
[2] ¶ The palace trees weep at night. The White River turns red with blood. Toads gather in the tops of the trees by the ten thousand. Storm winds, rain, lightning, and black clouds fighting like dragons over the temples. Last, a ghost runs into the palace shouting, and burrows into the ground. They dig, and find a turtle.
[3] ¶ They bring the turtle to the king in a lacquer box. He turns it over in his hands like a forgery he is pricing.
[4] King Euija: Three feet down, under my own palace. / Who buried you, little one? / …Hm. Somebody with good taste in shells.
[5] ▼ FLASHBACK 659 A room in Surabol, some months earlier
    [5.0] King Muyeol: For twenty years Euija has been selling his people miracles. / Dragons. White deer.
    [5.1] Kim Yushin: Knowing they were false?
    [5.2] King Muyeol: He made them himself. / Which makes him the worst reader of signs alive. / He has spent his whole life knowing that signs are made by hands.
    [5.3] Kim Yushin: …Then why would it work on him?
    [5.4] King Muyeol: It doesn’t have to work on him. / It only has to work on his people.
    [5.5] ¶ He does not order any of it, exactly. He asks for men who can travel, he asks what the markets of Sabi are frightened of, and he asks how deep one has to bury a turtle shell for the finding of it to look like an accident.
    [5.6] King Muyeol: An army is the last thing you need to bring down a country. / First you need a rumour. / And you build a rumour out of what the people are already afraid of.
[5] ▲ end flashback
[6] Baekje: Baekje falls! Baekje falls!
[7] ── SCENE: The Shaman ──
[8] ¶ He keeps a shaman on retainer the way other kings keep song-girls. He likes watching someone else believe the sky talks; he has told Gyebek the gods are cheap civil servants, and told Gesomun the same with wine on his breath. The shaman thinks he is frightened. He lets her.
[9] King Euija: I came for amusement today. / There are nine. / Read them.
[10] The Shaman: The foxes — the politicians are corrupt. / The hen and the sparrow — public morals have declined. / The great fish — the economy is in decline. / The great woman’s corpse — the people suffer for it.
[11] The Shaman: The ghost-screams — the forgotten common man cries out. / The blood-red river — the public sphere is polluted. / The toads in the trees — only lying peddlers have loud voices. / The dragon-clouds — the nation begins fighting itself.
[12] King Euija: …The turtle. / From the shell.
[13] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 20 (660); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 386): They obtained a tortoise; on its back was writing that said: Baekje is like the full moon; Silla is like the new moon.❞
[14] The Shaman: To be like a full moon is to be full — and what is full must wane — / to be like a crescent is to be not yet full — and what is not yet full grows fuller. / Baekje wanes. Silla fills.
[15] King Euija: You wretch!!!
[16] ¶ The blade is out before the last word cools. He cuts her down where she sits. The turtle’s sentence stays in the room.
[17] ¶ People start saying it out loud in the markets, which is how you know it is already over.
[18] Satek Chunbok: Your Majesty. What you need right now is not wine.
[19] Satek Chunbok: Your Majesty… / Say one name. / I will go and bring him.
[20] King Euija: …That name was one I made up. / When I was a prince on a mudbank.
[21] Satek Chunbok: …Your Majesty.
[22] King Euija: What are they saying in the markets these days.
[23] Satek Chunbok: …That Baekje is the full moon.
[24] King Euija: …Yes. / Well made.
[25] ¶ He never says that the signs were made. He could name the price of every piece of it. To say _a man made this one_ is to say it about the dragon over the Sabi, and the white deer, and the twenty years in between.
[26] ¶ The best lie a man ever tells is the one he cannot afford to expose.
[27] ── SCENE: The White River ──
[28] ¶ That night he leaves the palace the way he left it as a boy — without asking, without banners. The White River is waiting where it always waited. The omen said it ran red. Under the moon it is only black water and the smell of wet stone.
[29] ¶ He has spent years drowning on dry land: wine, women, and a letter he never sent to the man he never sent for. The river does not care. It knew him before the crown.
[30] King Euija: I named you here. / I will not die drunk on the bank of my own invention.
[31] ¶ He jumps. The cold takes the wine off him. When he surfaces he is coughing, furious, awake — the promising prince the eight clans once feared, scraped clean by the same river that taught him friendship.
[32] King Euija: Summon Gyebek…!
[33] ¶ Chunbok has followed him down with a lamp, the way a careful man follows a king who might be about to do something historic. He holds out a dry robe. The king does not take it.
[34] Satek Chunbok: Majesty, you’ll catch your death— / As Your Majesty well knows, a boat to Tamla takes time. / And the markets… forgive me. The markets are asking whether there will be a Baekje for him to come home to.
[35] King Euija: Let them ask. / We were a younger son’s house from the very start, Chunbok. Goguryeo got the hall. We got the road south. / Seven hundred years on a borrowed road, and we’re still here.
[36] Satek Chunbok: …For now, Majesty.
[37] King Euija: ‘For now.’ Ha. / That’s exactly what they told the first one, too.
[38] ¶ **Will Baekje survive? To answer that, go back to how it began: a mother, two sons, and a father who already had one…!**
