#67 Onjo  (-18)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: michuhol · tone: founder fairy tale
Logline: Nobody in their father’s hall ever mentions Buyeo. Then a boy with a sling turns up.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Every child in Baekje can tell you this story. Most of them get the beginning wrong.
[1] ¶ Onjo and Biryu grow up princes in their father’s hall. Nobody there ever mentions Buyeo.
[2] [MAP -18: ]
[3] ── SCENE: Buyeo ──
[4] ¶ In Buyeo, **Lady Ye** has raised Jumong’s first son alone.
[5] ¶ **Yuri** is a boy with a sling and bad aim, or good aim and bad luck. The pebble cracks a woman’s water jar on her way back from the well.
[6] [CARD King Yuri: Yuri. Bad aim or bad luck, and a mother who will not answer one question.]
[7] Water-carrier: Whose son are you, anyway? No father, no manners.
[8] King Yuri: What kind of man was my father? Where is he now?
[9] Lady Ye: Your father was no ordinary man. The country couldn’t hold him. / He went south and made himself a king. / He left something under the pine on the seven-sided stone. / Find it, and he’ll know you.
[10] ¶ There is no pine on any hill he climbs. He finds it at home: the house’s pine pillar stands on a seven-sided foundation stone, and in the crack beneath it lies half a sword.
[11] Lady Ye: Yuri….!
[12] ¶ With his friends, three boys as stubborn as he is, he walks his father’s road backwards, south.
[13] ── SCENE: The Half Sword ──
[14] ¶ In the hall at Jolbon he lays the half-sword on the boards. Jumong goes to a chest nobody has opened since the river, takes out the other half, and kneels. The two halves click.
[15] King Yuri: Father…!
[16] ¶ Onjo and Biryu watch from the porch rail. The rail already knows what the hall will decide.
[17] ── SCENE: The Last Night ──
[18] ¶ When Yuri is named crown prince, Sosuno does not fight the hall. She packs her dusty-rose silk. She packs the boys. She leaves the well.
[19] ¶ Jumong finds her at the old well, two buckets that have outlived the argument. Twenty winters in the same yard. He is still grinning. She is still pretending she came for water.
[20] Jumong: Hey. / You’re packed. / That’s… a lot of buckets for one road.
[21] Sosuno: Not buckets. / Grain. Boys. Me.
[22] Jumong: I left iron under a pine. I didn’t think it would grow up and walk in—
[23] Sosuno: Don’t— don’t make a speech. I’ll hit you.
[24] Jumong: Wasn’t going to. / Well’s still here. / I kept it. For you. Stupid, I know.
[25] Sosuno: Don’t be nice. / I’ll get stupid. / Yuri can have the chair. I’m not sitting in a footnote. / You know that. You always knew.
[26] Jumong: Yeah. / South, then. / Take the glow. Leave me the well. / …Come here. Please. One night. I’m still thirsty.
[27] Sosuno: Big idiot. / The boys are asleep. / If you compliment me I will scream. / …That’s not a no.
[28] ¶ They do not make it to a feast. They make it to the grain room that has been theirs since the first night, and she kisses him before the door is shut.
[29] ¶ Older. Hungrier. The hide has been off for years and she is worse now, not better.
[30] Jumong: Still you. / Still that mouth. / Look at you. Older. Better. Sorry. Not sorry.
[31] Sosuno: Don’t— ha— don’t you dare be sweet now. / Twenty winters, and you still breathe like you ran here. / …Slower. No. Not slower. / I want to remember this one. I’m not getting another.
[32] Jumong: Then don’t count. / I’ll count. / You know I’m bad at it.
[33] Sosuno: I hate you. I hate you, don’t stop— / …Say it. The thing you never say. / Say it now, while I can’t hit you.
[34] ¶ He says it into her hair. Even the sky looks away for this part. She laughs, and then she doesn’t, and the lamp burns down to a coal.
[35] Jumong: There. / Now you have to come back someday and hit me for it.
[36] ¶ Before dawn the lamp is out, and neither of them has slept.
[37] Sosuno: Don’t be nice. / I’ll get stupid. / …I’m already stupid. / Keep the well. I’m taking the glow.
[38] Jumong: Take it. / You’re beautiful. / Go found the other one. I’ll be here. Grinning. Like an idiot.
[39] ── SCENE: The Road South ──
[40] ¶ At dawn ten men start packing carts before anyone tells them to. Onjo and Biryu take their mother south. She walks like a woman who has been thoroughly answered and will not explain it to a deer, a son, or a chronicle.
[41] ¶ Three days south of the river, on a ridge path too narrow for the cart, a stag is standing in the way. Pale as mulberry paper, gold wherever the light touches it, antlers branching like a winter tree somebody decided to keep. It does not run. It looks at the three of them as if it had been told to expect three.
[42] Biryu: Don’t move. / That’s dinner for ten ministers. The antlers alone, a month of—
[43] Onjo: Hyung. Hyung, wait. / …That look like dinner to you? Really?
[44] Biryu: Looks like antlers to me. Meat with antlers.
[45] Sosuno: Biryu. Lower it. / …Listen to your mother. Bow down.
[46] ¶ Biryu lowers the bow the way an elder son does, slowly enough that everyone understands it was his own idea. The stag turns, walks ten paces up the ridge, and stops to look back. When they do not follow, it waits. When they do, it walks on. It keeps that up for nine days.
[47] Onjo: It wants us to follow, right? / …A deer knows the way, Mother?
[48] Sosuno: Your father crossed a river on turtles’ backs. / A deer’s practically civilised.
[49] ── SCENE: Mount Buak ──
[50] ¶ On the ninth day it takes them up Mount Buak, and from the top the brothers see all of it: a river looped across the plain like a belt somebody has unbuckled, high peaks at their backs, wet green flats to the south and, somewhere past the haze, the sea. Biryu smells the salt before he sees it.
[51] Biryu: Smell that? Sea. I’m going there. / River in front, mountains behind, sure, lovely. You can’t float a ship on it.
[52] Onjo: Hyung, all ten of them say here. / …I mean, ten people can all be wrong, but all ten—
[53] Biryu: Then the ten can live here. / And Mother? Who’s Mother coming with?
[54] Sosuno: …Don’t ask me that.
[55] ¶ Nobody answers him. The stag, which has stood a little apart all morning, crosses the summit and lies down in the grass at Onjo’s feet, facing the river. Biryu laughs too loudly and says the deer has no taste, and takes his half of the people down to Michuhol and the salt flats. The stag stays. Baekje will call it **Sinrok**, the guardian deer, for as long as Baekje has anything to call.
[56] [PLACE michuhol: Salt flats and sea wind. Biryu calls it a view.]
[57] Onjo: The land of ten tribes… Sipje! Hey, c’mon… we can think bigger than that. The land of a HUNDRED tribes… Baekje! Now that’s more like it….
[58] Onjo: “Baekje” — how does that sound?
[59] ¶ Biryu takes the sea. Onjo takes the river. Up north, their half-brother Yuri keeps the chair, and his line keeps it after him.
[60] ¶ So that is the family joke Euija and Gesomun used to throw at each other over wine. Goguryeo and Baekje are one father’s sons. One got the hall. One got the road. Neither has forgiven the other since.
[61] ¶ Seven hundred years later, the road ends at a riverbank in Sabi. Onjo’s heir is wringing the White River out of his sleeves. He once said a country is a territory governed by a single story. This was the story. He is about to learn who else can tell it.
[62] ¶ **Back to Sabi. Two armies are on the road, the boat for Gyebek still hasn’t sailed, and the king wants to know why…!**

=================================================================
#68 Sungchung  (660)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: sabi · tone: tragic loyalty drama
Logline: Two armies are coming for the capital, one by sea and one over the hills. The markets already have a name for it.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The war reaches Sabi the way bad news always does: through the fish market first.
[1] ¶ Two armies are coming for the capital, one by sea and one over the hills. The fishwives already have a name for it: the Chunchu Army. The king hears it from a maid, who heard it from a fishwife.
[2] ── SCENE: The Hall ──
[3] ¶ Euija holds court for the first time in three years. Half the benches are his sons. They watch him the way sons watch a father who has come home sober: politely, and counting the exits.
[4] King Euija: The boat for Gyebek. / I gave that order on a riverbank, soaking wet, in front of witnesses. / Where is he?
[5] Satek Chunbok: Your Majesty… as Your Majesty well knows, the winter crossings are— / And then the spring winds were—
[6] King Euija: The winds. A whole year of winds. / Chunbok. Do you take me for a fool, or for a drunk?
[7] Satek Chunbok: Majesty, by Onjo’s shrine, we have too few troops to send General Gyebek! / The Satek house lost its benches, not its levies. Better to wait for Lord Satek’s men…
[8] King Euija: **Who is the Eraha of this country?!** / **Buyeo Euija?** / **Or Minister Satek?** / **Send him NOW!**
[9] ¶ Chunbok bows very low, which is what he does instead of answering. A boat leaves for Tamla that afternoon. It is the fastest in the harbour. It is a year late.
[10] ── SCENE: The Letter ──
[11] ¶ That night the king does something he has not done in three years. He goes looking for a piece of paper.
[12] ¶ It is where he left it in the banquet hall, under a wine jar, with a red ring where the jar stood. The maids watch him lift the jar. Nobody giggles.
[13] The Court Maids: Majesty… that’s the councillor’s. / We didn’t throw it away. / We didn’t know if we were allowed to.
[14] King Euija: Read it to me. / My eyes are— just read it.
[15] The Court Maids: ‘A loyal servant does not forget his king even in death—’ / Majesty, then it’s a river and a pass. / ‘Do not let them cross Chimhyeon by land. Do not let their ships into Final Ford.’ / …Then just his name.
[16] King Euija: Chimhyeon. The soldiers call it Tanhyeon. / He told me the pass and the river three years ago. Starving. Through that wall. / And I put a jar on him.
[17] The Court Maids: Majesty—
[18] King Euija: Somebody else said this. Before him. Smiling at me, quoting sutras— / …Heungsu.
[19] ── SCENE: The Back of the Hall ──
[20] ¶ Next morning the provincial lords are summoned too, even the ones nobody has ever summoned.
[21] ¶ At the back of the hall, the lord of Bear Fortress says nothing. Ye Sikjin is doing the sum every provincial lord is doing. How many days from the river mouth to the capital? And how many from the capital to his own gate?
[22] King Euija: Lord Ye! Bear Fortress! Four generations and I never once asked you to court. My mistake. / How many men can you give me?
[23] Ye Sikjin: Your Majesty is generous to say so. / Bear Fortress will do exactly what is needed, Majesty. The number depends on the road.
[24] King Euija: Every number depends on the road. Give me one.
[25] Ye Sikjin: …As many as the road allows, Majesty.
[26] ¶ Euija laughs, because a king has to laugh at something before noon. Ye Sikjin bows exactly as low as the man beside him. That afternoon he rides home to Bear Fortress and opens a drawer.
[27] ¶ **One man might still know what to do. Euija sent him away too. Somebody ride. Now…!**

=================================================================
#69 Heungsu  (660)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: sabi · tone: tragic loyalty drama
Logline: The king sends for the one man he sent away for being right.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Heungsu has drawn the same map in the dirt every morning for three years. Today the king has finally sent someone to look at it.
[1] ▼ FLASHBACK 657–660 Gomamiji
    [1.0] ¶ The county is a day’s ride from the sea and a month from anyone who matters. Heungsu arrives with one chest and his office sword, hangs the sword on the doorpost, and on the first morning, before the clerk has finished his bow, scratches a map into the packed earth of the yard with the end of a broom handle.
    [1.1] ¶ A coastline. One river mouth, the White River’s, drawn twice as wide as it is. One notch in the eastern hills for **Tanhyeon**. Sabi as a thumbprint. Every morning the chickens and the children walk it out of shape, and every morning he sweeps it flat and draws it again, the same lines in the same order, like a monk at his morning sutra.
    [1.2] ?: Mister, is that a snake?
    [1.3] Heungsu: A river.
    [1.4] ?: What river?
    [1.5] Heungsu: One I hope you never see.
    [1.6] ¶ Nobody from Sabi writes. The news about Sungchung comes a season after the cell, on a salt boat, folded in between the price of salt and the price of rice, and the clerk reads it out because he reads everything out.
    [1.7] ?: The councillor in Sabi. The one who— in the cell. / …Was he someone you knew, sir?
    [1.8] Heungsu: …Better handwriting than mine.
    [1.9] ¶ That morning he does not draw the map. The next morning he does, and adds nothing to it, which the clerk takes as grief and the children take as permission to walk on Tanhyeon.
    [1.10] ¶ In the last year the rumours come down the coast faster than the salt: foxes in the Ministers’ Assembly, a river gone red. Heungsu hears each one out and goes back to his broom.
[1] ▲ end flashback
[2] ── SCENE: The Courier ──
[3] ¶ The courier does not sit. Dust is still on him. The sword on the doorpost is the only bright thing in the yard.
[4] ¶ He has stopped in the middle of the yard, which is to say in the middle of the map.
[5] The Courier: His Majesty asks. / The matter is urgent. What then.
[6] Heungsu: …Sungchung already wrote it. / Same paper. I don’t have a second one.
[7] The Courier: …That is all? / His Majesty asked for a plan, sir. Not a—
[8] Heungsu: You’re standing on Tanhyeon.
[9] ¶ The courier looks down and steps off a notch in the dirt, as if it might give way under him.
[10] Heungsu: And Gyebek? / Has anybody sent for Gyebek?
[11] The Courier: A boat went for him this week, sir. To Tamla.
[12] Heungsu: This week. / Five years, and this week.
[13] ¶ He looks down at the river mouth he has drawn too wide, and remembers the last time he saw the man they have finally sent for.
[14] ▼ FLASHBACK 655 The berth
    [14.0] ¶ It was a berth on Satek water, the afternoon the clans put Gyebek on a boat. Heungsu still had his office then. He came down to the water because nobody else from court did.
    [14.1] [CARD Heungsu: A Baekje minister sent far from court for saying what the king didn’t want to hear.]
    [14.2] ¶ Gyebek’s wife came too, with their boy at her side and a small girl on her hip. She had packed his bag. He had unpacked it on the dock and packed it again, in order.
    [14.3] Heungsu: You… you truly mean to go? / Without a word to the king—
    [14.4] Gyebek: The king is in mourning. He cannot sign. / The order has his seal. I am a loyal servant of Baekje.
    [14.5] Gyebek: His Majesty gave me a name. / A name — to a child who had none. / If he wants it back, he will send for it.
    [14.6] Gyebek’s Son: Father. How many days is Tamla?
    [14.7] Gyebek: Four, with a good wind.
    [14.8] Gyebek’s Son: Then I’ll count to four.
    [14.9] Gyebek: Count to five. The wind is not always good.
    [14.10] Heungsu: …Do you know the story of the Guardian of Ansi?
    [14.11] Gyebek: I do. / One person to cherish. One person to serve.
    [14.12] Gyebek: My trouble is that for me they are the same person.
    [14.13] ¶ His wife was standing close enough to hear it. She shifted the girl to her other hip and looked at the water. Heungsu has never forgotten that she did not look surprised.
    [14.14] Heungsu: Then hear one thing that is not a story. / If they ever send for you, hold the White River mouth and the Tanhyeon pass — or there will be no Sabi left to be loyal to. / The Tang do not need our clans’ permission to land. They need our absence.
    [14.15] Gyebek: I know the roads. / Yellow Mountain first — if that door holds, the river still has a kingdom behind it. / If it does not… then the berths you all fought over will belong to whoever can spell our names.
    [14.16] ¶ Then the captain with the Yunbi contract called the tide. Gyebek stepped aboard and did not look back, because looking back was not on the list. The boy counted out loud until the sail was gone. He got to four hundred and something before his mother made him stop.
[14] ▲ end flashback
[15] Heungsu: Tell His Majesty— / …No. He has the paper.
[16] ── SCENE: Sabi ──
[17] ¶ The answer comes back to Sabi. The ministers do not like the source.
[18] Satek Chunbok: Majesty, Heungsu is a man in exile. He resents his lord. / A man who resents his lord has no love of country. As Your Majesty well knows, his words must not be used.
[19] A Minister: Let them in, Majesty. / Let the Tang come up the river single file, with no room to spread their boats. Let Silla climb Tanhyeon, a path too narrow for two horses abreast. / Then strike. Chickens in a basket. Fish in a net.
[20] King Euija: Chickens in a basket. / …Ha. That’s good. That’s the kind of thing I used to think of. / Heungsu would say—
[21] Satek Chunbok: Heungsu says what Sungchung said, Majesty. / And Your Majesty did not take Sungchung’s advice either.
[22] ¶ It is very quiet. To take the advice now, the king would have to admit what it cost the last man who gave it. Kings will pay almost anything not to admit that.
[23] King Euija: So it is.
[24] ¶ The next courier is shorter. Tang keels are already in the mud of Final Ford. Yushin is already on the switchback. The White River and the Tanhyeon pass are already theirs.
[25] ¶ No second courier comes to Gomamiji. Heungsu sweeps the yard and draws the map for eleven more mornings, the river mouth still twice as wide as it is, because nobody has told him it is already full of Tang keels.
[26] ¶ On the twelfth it rains, and he stands under the eave and watches the White River and Tanhyeon run together into one brown puddle. He does not draw them again. He lifts the sword off the doorpost and starts north on foot, toward a pass that has already been crossed.
[27] ¶ The histories do not mention him again.
[28] ¶ **Across the sea, a boat is coming for the Turtle. He is on the shore before they finish tying it up…!**

=================================================================
#70 Gyebek  (660)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: sabi · tone: tragic loyalty drama
Logline: Somewhere in the fourth year he notices he has stopped counting the days. Then a boat comes.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Somewhere in the fourth year he notices he has stopped counting the days. It frightens him for a week. Then it does not.
[1] ¶ He stops correcting the people who call him Turtle, and carries water for the women who dive. He cannot write home. He never learned. Some evenings he counts to five on the beach, out loud, for a boy the island cannot see. For the first and last time in his life, he is in a place where being exactly what he is costs him nothing.
[2] ¶ A boat comes for him in the fifth year. He is on the shore before they finish tying it up.
[3] The Boatman: General Gyebek? / His Majesty’s words. He made me say them back to him twice. / ‘The river was cold. I went in. Come home.’
[4] Gyebek: …That is three things.
[5] The Boatman: Sir?
[6] Gyebek: He said three things. I heard all three.
[7] Yuri Dora: Turtle. What is the hurry. / You could die comfortable here.
[8] Gyebek: Nothing here is mine to keep.
[9] Yuri Dora: Then what is yours.
[10] Gyebek: …A promise.
[11] ¶ He takes nothing off the island except the stories, which is the only export it has ever had.
[12] Yuri Dora: Turtle. Learn one thing before you go. / A story is not begun with its ending already fixed.
[13] Gyebek: …Mine is fixed.
[14] ¶ Five years of listening, and that is the one lesson that does not take.
[15] ¶ He says goodbye at the water. It takes longer than he planned.
[16] Yuri Dora: Gyebek! It gladdened me to know a man like you. / Once you go back to the mainland, who knows if we shall meet again. / Promise me just one thing. / Do not forget people.
[17] Gyebek: …My lord. I was a child with no family and no name. / The crown prince of a kingdom gave me a name, and asked if I liked it. / I am an ignorant man who cannot even read. / But as a man, I will keep faith.
[18] ── SCENE: Sabi ──
[19] ¶ He lands at the White River mouth and rides to the palace without changing his clothes. The guards do not know his face any more. The king does.
[20] ¶ Euija meets him in the yard, not the hall. He is thinner, and sober, and sobriety does not suit him yet. For a moment neither of them says anything, which for Euija is some kind of record.
[21] King Euija: Turtle! / That’s what they call you down there, isn’t it? The boatman told me. / Ha— it suits you. You look like you’ve been living under a rock.
[22] Gyebek: Five years. / Your Majesty sent for me after four.
[23] King Euija: …I wrote it the night of the Assembly. / I didn’t send it. The houses were counting, and a careful man said wait a month, and I— / I’m a king. I don’t explain myself twice.
[24] Gyebek: You explained it once.
[25] King Euija: Then that’s my allowance spent!
[26] ¶ He laughs first, the way he always does. Then he tells him the rest the way a king gives orders. Tang ships for the river mouth. Silla on the eastern road. Fifty thousand between them. He does not pretend that five thousand is enough.
[27] King Euija: Five thousand. That’s the whole purse. / The Satek levies are ‘on the way’. They’ve been on the way for a year.
[28] Gyebek: Where.
[29] King Euija: Wherever you judge. / You remember what I told you. The last time.
[30] Gyebek: ‘One day I will give you a stupid order. Judge it yourself.’ / ‘You are still the king of your own life.’
[31] King Euija: Word for word. Of course. / This isn’t a stupid order. It’s just a bad one. / You don’t owe me this. The name was a gift.
[32] Gyebek: I gave my word.
[33] King Euija: …You asked me once whether I liked the name, or you. / I never answered.
[34] Gyebek: No.
[35] King Euija: Both. / Now go, before I say something royal.
[36] ¶ Gyebek bows and turns. He is at the gate when the king calls after him.
[37] King Euija: Gyebek— your house. Your wife, the children. / Send them to Bear Fortress. Lord Ye’s walls are thick.
[38] Gyebek: If Sabi falls, no wall in Baekje is thick.
[39] King Euija: …Then judge it yourself. You always do.
[40] ¶ It is the kindest thing he can think of to say. Gyebek, who takes every word exactly as it is given, takes it home.
[41] ── SCENE: Home ──
[42] ¶ Before he marches he goes home. His wife is in the yard. She has heard; the whole street has heard. She does not ask how many. She has been married to him long enough to know he will tell her the exact number.
[43] Gyebek: Five thousand. Against fifty.
[44] Gyebek’s Wife: …The boy has been counting since the boat was sighted. / He won’t stop until you tell him.
[45] Gyebek’s Son: Father! Nine thousand, four hundred and— and twelve!
[46] Gyebek: You can stop.
[47] Gyebek’s Son: Was it right?
[48] Gyebek: Yes.
[49] ¶ His wife looks at him for a long time. Then she takes the children inside and leaves the door open, and he goes in after them.
[50] ¶ What he does there he does so that nothing of his can be used against him. The histories record it in one line.
[51] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 47, Biographies, Gyebaek): I fear my wife and children will be taken and made slaves. Better a quick death than a life of shame. And so he killed them all.❞
[52] ¶ He comes out before the light is properly up. The yard is swept. Nothing in it is his any more except a black horse at the post. Gomanari is named for the bear ferry where Gyebek learned to ride. It is the one thing he owns that the Tang cannot sell in a slave market.
[53] ¶ The groom, a boy from the next village who did not sleep in the house and is therefore alive, holds the bridle out at arm’s length and will not look at him.
[54] ?: H-here, General. / …Gomanari too?
[55] Gyebek: A horse can’t be made a slave. / A horse is just a horse.
[56] ¶ He saddles it himself, counting the buckles under his breath, and when he is done he stands with his forehead against the black neck for exactly as long as it takes to count to ten. Then he mounts and does not look at the house.
[57] ── SCENE: The March ──
[58] ¶ Gyebek and his five thousand set out for the Yellow Mountain. It is the last latch on the road to Sabi. Merchants have cursed its summer dust for years.
[59] ¶ They are waiting at the crossroads outside the city: farmers’ sons, old border men, a few who stood on the mudbank the day a prince named a boy. Nobody cheers. Somebody holds out a spare spear. Gyebek takes it, and counts them row by row before he says a word.
[60] Gyebek: Long live Baekje….!
[61] ¶ **Somewhere, Kangrim closes his ledger on a swept yard. Then he goes up to a meeting with one question he shouldn’t ask…!**

=================================================================
#71 Three Realms  (태초)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Epilogue · place: realms_pavilion · tone: divine comedy
Logline: Once a year the gods meet in a pavilion on the clouds. This year the reaper comes late from a swept yard in Baekje, with a question about the dead.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Once a year the gods hold a meeting. Kangrim is late to this one, because of a yard in Baekje.
[1] ¶ The annual meeting is a small pavilion: four posts, a raised floor, clouds for a yard. Living, dead and western rows all fit if nobody stretches.
[2] [PLACE realms_pavilion: Four posts, clouds for a yard, and very strict seating.]
[3] [DIAGRAM pantheon:courts The Three Realms · 삼계 — Hwanin above; Living, Dead, and Western Flower Field below. Heaven is not a fourth peer realm.]
[4] ¶ Before the principals sit — servants first. The Three Realms under the Big Man Upstairs still gossip like any court.
[5] Haemosu: Ah, Kangrim…. Looking as young as ever, eh?
[6] Kangrim: Shut it, sun. I’ve had a long morning.
[7] Yumla: H-hey, Samsin.
[8] Samsin: Oh, long time no see, Yumla! How's the Underworld these days?
[9] Yumla: Y-you know… full of dead people.
[10] ¶ Then the midwife and the sun find the same rail. The rest of the pavilion develops a sudden, devout interest in clouds.
[11] Samsin: Hey, Haemosu. / Did you see Yumla’s face? Went straight purple. / And I barely hiked the skirt.
[12] Haemosu: Barely? I felt that from the chariot. / Anyone in this pavilion hungrier than us? Name one.
[13] Samsin: Ibiga? He flirts with weather. / Kangrim stares at his notebook. Yumla goes purple if I breathe. / We’re the only ones actually hot in here. / Man or not — I like that I can gossip like this with you.
[14] Kangrim: …Nothing for the ledger. / And that’s correct.
[15] ¶ Then the principals duck the lintel — Hallakgungi alone, Big Star with his dark court, Little Star with sky and sun and birth.
[16] ¶ The pavilion was not built for three sovereignties. They sit anyway.
[17] Hallakgungi: Hey Little Star… didn’t the Big Man Upstairs send his son down to the mortal domain a while back? / Whatever happened to him?
[18] Little Star: Speaking of which… / Big things are happening in the mortal realm. / The mortals are starting to speak of reunifying Dangun's kingdom.
[19] Big Star: …
[20] Hallakgungi: Elder brother of the dead goes quiet again. / In my field, resurrection and ruin grow in the same rows. Reunification probably does too.
[21] ¶ Kangrim has not sat down. This morning he collected a woman and two children from a swept yard in Baekje. The girl asked if her father was coming too. Kangrim does not lie, so he said, “Later.” He has been thinking about the flower field ever since.
[22] Kangrim: Sir.
[23] Hallakgungi: Yes?
[24] Kangrim: I've always been curious… what sorts of flowers grow in your fields?
[25] Hallakgungi: Haha… well, there are those that regenerate new blood, grow new skin, grow new bones… / To be honest, I can't even keep track of all of them anymore. / Why do you ask?
[26] ❝QUOTE (Segyeong Bonpuri (세경본풀이) recited by Lee Seung-sun (이승순), recorded by Gang Jeong-sik, Gang So-jeon and Song Jeong-hui, 2011 — Sanggari, Aewol-eup (Hanguk Gubimunhak Daegye, rev. ed.)): “Seeing the Western Flower Field — what flower is this?” “The flower that gives back speech. This one, the flower that brings blood back. The flower that brings flesh back, the one for the organs and bowels, the flower that brings bones back.”❞
[27] Kangrim: I was just curious… using all of these flowers at once… / Is it… is it possible to resurrect a dead person?
[28] ¶ Hallakgungi’s face hardens.
[29] Hallakgungi: Grim Reaper Kangrim. What is this line of questioning? / Do you have something you need to tell me?
[30] Kangrim: No, sir. I was—
[31] Hallakgungi: Well, to answer your question. It is possible. / I've done it… only for one person. / But I do not get involved in mortal affairs.
[32] Kangrim: Only one. / …And who decides which one?
[33] Hallakgungi: I do. Cheerfully. And I already have. / Rule of the field, reaper: pick a flower for one mortal and the whole row wilts. Sit down.
[34] ¶ Kangrim sits down at the end of the dead’s row. He opens his ledger to a page headed Yellow Mountain, and does not like how long it is.
[35] Little Star: I cheated for the living world. / Them cutting each other… that is my small law too. / Still — when they call Dangun’s name again, does the Big Man Upstairs laugh, or sigh?
[36] Big Star: Let the meeting begin. / Business of the living… last item on the agenda.
[37] ¶ **The minutes of that meeting never leave Heaven’s table. Down below, five thousand men are counting fifty thousand…!**
